title: A Story
sections_statement: Once upon a time in a world that looks like ours a story of a person who looks like many of us is about to begin and it unravels like a jigsaw puzzle. Make sure to open your eyes and focus, as things can look like a duplicated version of another person's story but soon you will know that it is exceptionally different than any other story you've experienced. For it being a great harmonic and very imminent journey where paths may cross. Kudos to those who hone their knowledge and leverage their skills as marching into the future would definitely require them. Esraa is working as an information security engineer. Every employee in her company has a password which is a permutation of N integers. All the passwords are stored on the main server. To ensure their safety, Esraa created an encryption algorithm and named it EsraaCipher, the algorithm works in the following way: 1. The algorithm appends a 0 to the end of the permutation. 2. It generates all the rotations (left cyclic shifts) of the permutation. 3. It sorts the generated rotations in lexicographical increasing order. 4. The encrypted password is constructed by taking the last integer of every generated rotation after sorting lexicographically. Here is an example on how the algorithm works: suppose the permutation P is {2, 1}, first a 0 is appended to the end of P so it becomes {2, 1, 0}, now the algorithm will generate all the rotations which are: {2, 1, 0}, {1, 0, 2}, {0, 2, 1}. after sorting the rotations we get: {0, 2, 1}, {1, 0, 2}, {2, 1, 0}. the encrypted password is constructed by taking the last number of every rotation after sorting, so the resulting encrypted password is {1, 2, 0}. You are hired to try to decrypt and retrieve all the passwords. Can you write a program to decrypt all the T passwords (given the encrypted password, restore the original password)?
sections_input: The first line of input contains on integer T (1 ≤ T ≤ 10^5), the number of testcases (passwords to decrypt). The first line of every testcase contains one integer N (1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5), the length of the ith password. The second line of every testcase contains N + 1 integers separated by spaces, which represent the encrypted password. It's guaranteed that the encrypted password contains distinct integers and any integer x of them in the range [0, N ] (0 ≤ x ≤ N ). It's also guaranteed that the sum of lengths of all passwords won't exceed 3x105
sections_output: Output T lines, in the ith line output N integers separated by spaces which represent the ith password after decryption. Note that it must be a permutation of size N.

title: Begins and it
sections_statement: Just like any story, it begins with an ambitious person, Hisham. And as it moves forward, paths start to appear and connect. And as it takes two to Tango, Endure Capital, the ACPC Community Partner, believing in the relentless execution to build and achieve hyper-growth, starts investing in Hisham’s future journey. Hisham has two integer arrays A and B, both of length N. He defines the beautiful shifting operations on arrays x of length N as doing one of two operations: • Shift all elements to the right, i.e. the new value of x i is equal to the old value of x i-1 , and the new value of x 1 is equal to the old value of x N. • Shift all elements to the left, i.e. the new value of x i is equal to the old value of x i+1 , and the new value of x N is equal to the old value of x 1. Hisham calls index I beautiful if Bi divides Ai , i.e. (Ai mod Bi == 0). Also he defines the beauty of the array A as the number of beautiful indices. You can do the beautiful shifting to either A or B as many times as you want (possibly zero). What is the maximum possible beauty of Array A? It’s guaranteed that the elements of the array B are distinct.
sections_input: The first line of input contains one integer T (1 ≤ T ≤ 10^0), the number of testcases. The first line of every testcase contains one integer N (1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5), the length of the arrays A, B. The second line of every testcase contains N integers separated by spaces, which represent the array A (1 ≤ Ai ≤ 10^5). The third line of every testcase contains N integers separated by spaces, which represent the array B (1 ≤ Bi ≤ 10^5), and all Bi are distinct. It’s guaranteed that the sum of N over all testcases won’t exceed 3x105.
sections_output: Output T lines, in the ith line output one integer which represents the maximum possible beauty of arrays A for the ith testcase.

Note that: • the beauty value of a tree is equal to the sum of beauty values of all its vertices. • the beauty value of a forest is equal to the sum of beauty values of all its trees.

title: Diverse Culture of Al-Khalil
sections_statement: Al-Khalil beckons Aamer with its bustling markets and ancient streets, reflecting a city that has thrived as a cultural crossroads for over 4,000 years. Then follows Q lines. The i-th line contains three integers ti Li Ri. (ti ∈ {1, 2}, 1 ≤ Li ≤ Ri ≤ N ). Which represents the i-th query. It is guaranteed that there is at least one query of type 2.

title: Exploration of Jericho’s Oases
sections_statement: Jericho captivates Aamer with its ancient oases and desert landscapes, emblematic of a city steeped in over 10,000 years of human settlement. title: Fishing Traditions of Tiberias
sections_statement: Aamer explores Tiberias, where ancient fishing traditions intertwine with spiritual significance and healing practices dating back over 2,000 years. Set on the shores of the Sea of Galilee, Tiberias continues to embody a harmonious blend of nature, tradition, and spiritual renewal. sections_output: Output a single integer — the answer to the problem, taken modulo 109 + 7.

title: Gateways of Beisan
sections_statement: Beisan, known historically as Beit She’an, invites Aamer to uncover its archaeological wonders and strategic significance in the Jordan Valley. For over 5,000 years, Beisan’s ancient gateways have served as conduits of cultural exchange and testament to its enduring legacy as a pivotal junction of civilizations. Anas has a folder on his computer that has only one file. The file name is s that has n lowercase Latin letters numbered from 1 to n. Anas would like to do the following instructions every second until the system breaks: • Choose a random lowercase Latin letter x. • Make a new string t which is initially equal to s. • An integer number i (0 ≤ i ≤ n) is chosen randomly and x is inserted after the first i characters in t. For example, if t = “abc”, x = “d” and i = 1, then t would be “adbc”. • Add a new file in the folder with the name t. • If there is already a file with the name t, the system will break. Otherwise, Anas will repeat the process. Note that when Anas does multiple operations, they are all performed on the initial string s. In other words, all of the resulting strings t will be of length n + 1, so the operations don’t stack. What is the expected number of seconds until the system breaks?
sections_input: The first and only line of input contains a string s (1 ≤ |s| ≤ 10^4) where |s| is the length of string s. The initial file’s name. It is guaranteed that s contains only lowercase Latin letters.
sections_output: Print a single line containing a single integer — the expected number of seconds until the system breaks, taken modulo 109 + 7. It is guaranteed that the answer can always be represented as an irreducible fraction a , where b mod (109 + 7) /= 0; you have to print a · b−1 mod (109 + 7).

title: Harbor Life in Jaffa
sections_statement: Aamer immerses himself in the vibrant harbor life of Jaffa, where maritime activity has shaped its identity as a gateway for trade and cultural interaction. Navigating through its bustling waters, Jaffa’s strategic importance and historical role as a hub of connectivity come alive amidst the ebb and flow of commerce. You are given an array a of n integer numbers. You need to process q queries each of which follows one of the following formats: • 1 l r x. For each integer number ai where. (l ≤ i ≤ r), apply ai := ai&x, where & is the bitwise AND operator. • 2 i x. Apply ai := x. • 3 l r. For the subarray al, al+1, al+2 . . . ar, print the maximum XOR of a subset of integers of the subarray. A subarray is a contiguous part of the array. A subset of an array is a tuple that can be obtained from the array by removing some (possibly all) elements of it.
sections_input: The first line of the input contains a single integer number t (1 ≤ t ≤ 10^4) — The number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two space separated integer numbers n and q (1 ≤ n, q ≤ 10^5). The number of integer numbers of a and the number of queries, respectively. The second line of each test contains n space separated integer numbers ai (1 ≤ ai ≤ 10^5), where ai is the i − th integer number of a. Each of the following q lines follows one of the following formats. • 1 l r x (1 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n, 1 ≤ x ≤ 10^5). • 2 i x. (1 ≤ i ≤ n, 1 ≤ x ≤ 10^5). • 3 l r. (1 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n). It is guaranteed that the sum of n over all of the test cases does not exceed 105. It is guaranteed that the sum of q over all of the test cases does not exceed 105.
sections_output: For each query of the third type for each test case, print a single line containing a single integer number. The maximum XOR of a subset of integers of the subarray given in the query.

title: Interwoven Cultures of Nablus
sections_statement: Nablus’s winding streets and lively markets reflect a city that has flourished as a commercial and cultural center for over 2,000 years. Offering Aamer a glimpse into its history, he discovered how Nablus has been considered the main commercial and industrial center in Palestine, and even well-known for its sweets like Nabulsi Kunafa. You are given a string S of n Latin characters, and an array A of n integers. Each element has a value of Ai. Find the length of the longest good substring. A substring S[l, r] (1 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n) is considered good if both of the conditions below are true: 1. S[l, r] is a palindrome (Sl+i = Sr−i for all 0 ≤ i ≤ r − l) 2. Al|Al+1|...|Ar−1|Ar = Σr i=l Ai, where | is the bitwise OR operator. Noot: x|y means x bitwise or y.
sections_input: The first line contains the number of test cases (1 ≤ t ≤ 10^3). The first line of each test case contains n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5). The second line of each test case contains a string S of length n. The last line of each test case contains n space-separated integers A1, A2, ..., An (1 ≤ Ai ≤ 10^9) — the array A. It is guaranteed that the sum of n over all test cases does not exceed 3 · 105.
sections_output: For each test case, print one integer: The maximum length of a substring that fulfills both of the conditions above.

title: Journey in Safed’s Mysteries
sections_statement: Safed beckons Aamer with its mystical allure and spiritual significance, steeped in over 2,000 years of cultural and historical richness. As he navigates its winding alleys and sacred sites, Safed’s reputation as a spiritual beacon, offering moments of contemplation and discovery. Given an array a of length n, which may contain negative integers. We define the beauty of a prefix a[1, i] (1 ≤ i ≤ n) as the maximum possible subarray sum that can be obtained from that prefix by applying the following operation at most once: select two indices x and y (1 ≤ x, y ≤ i), and swap ax with ay. Your task is to find the beauty of each prefix of a.
sections_input: The first line of the input contains a single integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^6), representing the length of the array. The second line of the input contains n space-separated integers a1, a2, ..., an (−106 ≤ ai ≤ 10^6), representing the array a.
sections_output: Output one line containing n space-separated integers, representing the beauty of each prefix of a.

title: Kaleidoscope of Ramla’s Diversity
sections_statement: Ramla’s urban landscape reveals layers of cultural diversity and historical heritage spanning over 1,300 years. Founded during the early Islamic period, Ramla’s streets and markets showcase its role as a vibrant hub of trade, agriculture, and religious tolerance, shaped by centuries of multicultural influence. Majed didn’t understand why his parents always told him to turn off the lights when leaving a room, until he had kids and started paying the bills himself. Then, he realized how these small actions could save a lot of money. One day, Majed came home and saw that all the lights were on. He started telling his kids how this would waste a lot of money. He explained that leaving the lights on when no one is using them makes the electricity bill go up. Majed’s apartment has n lights. Each light i costs ai pounds per hour to keep on. To show his kids how much money they are wasting by leaving all the lights on, he needs to calculate the total cost of running all the lamps for one hour, but he’s not so good at math. Can you help him?
sections_input: The first line of the input contains a single integer number t (1 ≤ t ≤ 10). The number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains a single integer number n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5). The number of lamps in Majed’s apartment. The second line of each test case contains n space-separated integer numbers a1, a2...an, where ai (1 ≤ ai ≤ 10^4) is the cost of lighting the i − th lamp for an hour.
sections_output: For each test case, print a single line containing a single integer number. The total cost of lighting all the lamps for one hour.

title: Logistics of Lod’s Connectivity
sections_statement: The city of Lod is located to the southeast of the city of Jaffa, about 15 km away from it, and to the northeast of the city of Ramla, about 5 km away from it. Lod is 50 meters above sea level. It occupies an important position as it is a transportation node where railway lines meet and it is the meeting point of Jaffa, Haifa, Al-Quds and Egypt, and through it the traveler can move from Egypt to Palestine and then to Lebanon and Turkey. Ammar found 2 permutations a and b of length n. While he was taking them home, he lost exactly 1 element from each permutation but the elements didn’t change order. More formally, if the permutation was p1, p2, . . . , pn. And the ith element was lost, it becomes p1, p2, . . . , pi−1, pi+1, . . . , pn. Ammar doesn’t remember the initial permutations, but he wants you to restore any two permutations that have the maximum possible Σn i=1 |ai − bi| . If there are multiple answers, print any.
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer n (2 ≤ n ≤ 3 · 105) — the length of the original permutations. The second line contains n − 1 integers a (1 ≤ ai ≤ n) — the remaining elements of a. The third line contains n − 1 integers b (1 ≤ bi ≤ n) — the remaining elements of b. It is guaranteed that a and b are permutations with one element removed.
sections_output: On the first line print a single integer which is the maximum value of Σn i=1 |ai − bi| possible. Then, on the second and third lines print a and b respectively. If there are multiple answers, print any of them.

title: Majestic Crossroads Al-Nasserah
sections_statement: Al-Nasserah in the heart of Lower Galilee, overlooks the Marj Ibn Amer plain and serves as a transition between this plain and the mountainous Upper Galilee. Historically significant, it connected main roads between Syria, Egypt, Jordan, and Palestine, attracting commercial caravans. You are given an array a of n integer numbers. You need to answer q queries. In each query you are given an integer x. You need to count the number of subarrays al, al+1, al+2 . . . ar that satisfy for each i where l ≤ i < r, the inequality ai + (i − l) ∗ x ≤ ai+1 + (i − l + 1) ∗ x is satisfied.

The first line of each test case contains two space-separated integer numbers n and q (2 ≤ n ≤ 10^5) (1 ≤ q ≤ 10^5). The number of integer numbers in the array a and the number of queries, respectively. The second line of each test case contains n space-separated integer numbers a1, a2 . . . an (−109 ≤ ai ≤ 10^9), where ai is the i − th number in the array a. The third line of the input contains q space-separated integer numbers x1, x2 . . . xn (−109 ≤ xi ≤ 10^9), where xi is the parameter of the i − th query. It is guaranteed that the sum of n over all of the test cases does not exceed 105. It is guaranteed that the sum of q over all of the test cases does not exceed 105.
sections_output: For each test case print a single line containing q space-separated integer numbers, where the i−th number is the answer to the i − th query.

title: Navigation Challenges in Gaza
sections_statement: Gaza City’s turbulent history and strategic significance shape Aamer’s exploration of its intricate urban landscapes. Founded over 4,000 years ago, Gaza’s resilience amidst challenges reflects its enduring spirit and the complexities of navigating humanitarian aid and development in a dynamic and diverse environment. You are given an array a of length n. Let’s say that element ai eats element aj (i < j) if the range sum of array a from i to k for every k from i to j − 1 is greater than or equal to ak+1. More formally, ai eats aj if sumi,k ≥ ak+1 for (i ≤ k < j) where suml,r is the sum of array elements from l to r (al + al+1 + ... + ar). For more explanation, if the following is satisfied then ai eats aj: • ai ≥ ai+1 • ai + ai+1 ≥ ai+2 • ai + ai+1 + ai+2 ≥ ai+3 • .... • ai + .. + aj−1 ≥ aj We define distancej as the minimum value of j − i where i < j and ai can eat aj. In case there is no ai that eats aj, then the distance of aj is 0. Print the sum of distances of all array elements.

title: Urban Exploration in Al-Quds
sections_statement: Aamer embarks on a journey through Al-Quds, a city revered for over 4,000 years as a cultural and spiritual crossroads. From ancient paths to sacred sites, Al-Quds’s enduring significance and historical tapestry come alive, offering Aamer insights into its profound influence on global civilizations and faiths. We have n computers running on a system, the computers form a tree rooted at node 1. Each computer has a latency value. Let’s define the power of a computer as the minimum bitwise XOR between its latency and the latency of any computer of its ancestors. When a task is assigned to a computer, all computers in its subtree will work to finish this task. A computer will fail if it’s working on a number of tasks that exceeds its power. You have to answer q queries, each of them contains a computer, for each query: calculate the maximum number of tasks that could be assigned to this computer, such that all the computers in its subtree won’t fail (inculding itself).

The next line contains n − 1 integers p2, p3, ..., pn — the parents of computers from the second to the n − th (1 ≤ pi < i). Each of the next q lines contain a single integer computeri (2 ≤ computeri ≤ n), representing the queries.

title: Founder DNA Match - The Human Capital Engine
sections_statement: At the venture capital firm **Den VC**, building a successful startup starts with finding the right people. As part of Den VC's mission to invest in outstanding founders, you are tasked with helping the lead founder (Founder 1) choose the best possible co-founder from a list of $n$ candidates by maximizing a **synergy score**. A candidate founder $i$ ($i \ne 1$) is **eligible** only if they meet all of the following conditions compared to Founder 1: - They are in the **same city**. - They have a **different skill domain**. - They share the **same value system**. For each eligible candidate $i$, the **synergy score** is calculated as: $$ \mathrm{Score}_i=\mathrm{DiversityBonus}+(p_i\cdot p_1)+(r_i\cdot r_1)+(m_i\cdot m_1) $$ where $p$, $r$, and $m$ are the scores for Problem-Solving, Resourcefulness, and Imagination. The **DiversityBonus** is **+1000** if the two founders have opposite personality types (`introvert`/`extrovert`); otherwise, it is $0$. If no eligible co-founder exists, the output should be **-1**. *Sponsored by Den VC — investing in founders who change the world.*
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer $n$ ($2 \le n \le 1000$) — the total number of founders, including Founder 1 (the lead founder). Each of the next $n$ lines describes one founder in the following format: ``` City SkillDomain ValueSystem PersonalityType P R M ``` - `City` — a string of $1$ to $20$ lowercase English letters representing the founder's city. - `SkillDomain` — a string of $1$ to $20$ lowercase English letters representing their domain of expertise. - `ValueSystem` — a string of $1$ to $20$ lowercase English letters representing the founder's core values. - `PersonalityType` — either `introvert` or `extrovert`. - $P$, $R$, $M$ — integers ($0 \le P, R, M \le 100$) representing the founder's scores in Problem-Solving, Resourcefulness, and Imagination, respectively. The first of the $n$ lines always describes Founder 1. The remaining $n-1$ lines describe the candidate founders in order.
sections_output: Print a single integer — the maximum synergy score among all eligible candidates, or **-1** if none are eligible.
sections_notes: In the first example: - **Founder 1:** `cairo ai visionary introvert`. - **Founder 2:** Not eligible (different city and different value system). - **Founder 3:** Eligible (same city, different skill, same value). - **Founder 4:** Not eligible (same skill domain). Only Founder 3 is eligible. The synergy score is: $$ 1000 + (95 \times 80) + (60 \times 70) + (80 \times 90) = 20000. $$ In the second example, no candidate is eligible because Founder 2 has the same skill and a different value system. So the output is **-1**.

title: AI Archive: Project DIVISIA
sections_statement: Jaber is a passionate computer scientist who spends his nights training for national contests. One day, while experimenting with a quantum search engine powered by substring frequencies, Jaber stumbles upon a mysterious encrypted string $S$ embedded in an ancient archive labeled "Project DIVISIA". He learns that this archive holds massive language models trained on thousands of languages — but only one query format can be used to unlock the AI's next level of understanding. To decode a part of the AI, Jaber must feed it specially crafted string patterns and evaluate their behavior over parts of $S$. For each query, Jaber is given a pattern $t$, and he must measure how often $t$ appears in different parts of $S$. The AI evaluates how balanced the occurrences are by computing the greatest common divisor between the counts in different regions. But there's a twist — he must only compare non-intersecting regions of the string. To succeed, Jaber needs to find the maximum value of: $$ fgcd(cnt(t, l_1, r_1), cnt(t, l_2, r_2)) $$ over all valid, non-overlapping pairs $[l_1, r_1]$ and $[l_2, r_2]$. He knows that for this mission: - sub($l$, $r$) returns the substring $S_l, S_{l+1}, \dots, S_r$. - cnt($t$, $l$, $r$) is the number of substrings of sub($l$, $r$) that are equal to the string $t$. - fgcd($x$, $y$) returns the greatest common divisor of $x$ and $y$, with a special rule: $$ \mathrm{fgcd}(x, y) = \begin{cases} \gcd(x, y), & \text{if } x \neq 0 \text{ and } y \neq 0, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ Help Jaber complete all $Q$ queries and unlock the next level of Project DIVISIA.
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer number $T$, $(T \le 2*10^5)$ the number of testcases. Each testcase contains the following: The first line contains the string $S$, $(|S| \le 2*10^5)$ consisting only of lowercase English letters. The second line contains a single integer $Q$, $(Q \le 2*10^5)$, followed by $Q$ lines. The $i$-th of the $Q$ lines contains a string $t$, $(|t| \le 2*10^5)$. It is guaranteed that $\sum_{}|t| \le 2*10^5$ and $\sum_{}|S| \le 2*10^5$ and $\sum_{}Q \le 2*10^5$ all the queries and testcases.
sections_output: In each testcase, for each of the $Q$ queries, output the answer to the query in a separate line.

title: Houssain and George's XOR Expedition
sections_statement: Houssain and George are two brilliant cryptographers who discovered a hidden algorithm embedded deep within the oldest quantum chip ever made — the "X-Core." To unlock the chip's full processing power, they must solve a bitwise puzzle designed by the original engineers over 100 years ago. They are given an array $a$ of size $n$, encoded with ancient machine language. The chip challenges them to find the number of valid triplets $(i, j, k)$ such that $1 \le i \lt j \lt k \le n$ and the following condition is satisfied: $$ a_i \le a_i \oplus a_j \le a_i \oplus a_j \oplus a_k $$ This condition represents the increasing complexity of layered encryption, where $\oplus$ denotes the bitwise XOR operation. Only by finding all such valid triplets can they fully decrypt the chip's core secrets. Help Houssain and George complete their XOR expedition!
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer $T$ ($1 \le T \le 10^4$), the number of test cases. Then $T$ test cases follow. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 10^5$), the size of the array $a$. The second line of each test case contains $n$ positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ ($1 \le a_i \le 10^9$), the elements of the array. It is guaranteed that the sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $10^5$.
sections_output: For each test case, print a single integer representing the number of triples satisfying the conditions.

title: Amira and Ahmed's Birthday
sections_statement: Amira works in Business Development at ACPC. Her birthday is on the 22nd of August, and Ahmed, the son of Mohamed Fouad, has his birthday on the 23rd of August. This year, Mohamed Fouad decided to celebrate both birthdays together as one joyful occasion — but he's bringing only one cake. To decide who will get to blow out the birthday candle, Amira and Ahmed turn the celebration into a challenge. They prepare a sequence of $n$ party tasks to be done in order — some add joy, others bring stress. The party's happiness level starts at $0$. Each task either increases or decreases the happiness by a certain amount. The rule is simple: if the happiness level ever drops below 0, the party is considered ruined, and the opponent of the one who performed that task wins the right to blow out the candle. If all tasks are completed without the happiness level falling below $0$, the result is a draw, and they both share the celebration. Can you predict who will blow out the candle?
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer $n$ ($1 \leq n \leq 10^5$) — the number of tasks. Each of the next $n$ lines contains two integers $t_i$ and $v_i$: - $t_i$ is the task type ($1$ = increase happiness, $2$ = decrease happiness), - $v_i$ is the happiness value ($1 \leq v_i \leq 100$). Tasks alternate between Amira and Ahmed, starting with Amira. That is, task $1$ is Amira's, task $2$ is Ahmed's, and so on.
sections_output: - If the happiness level becomes negative at any point, print AHMED if it happened during Amira's task, or AMIRA if it happened during Ahmed's task. - If the happiness never goes below zero, print DRAW.

title: Baran and Thaer's Enchanted Lexicon
sections_statement: Baran and Thaer are two young linguists who stumbled upon a magical dictionary in the ruins of an ancient AI research lab. This dictionary contains $m$ powerful words, each composed only of lowercase English letters. As part of unlocking the secrets of the lexicon, they are faced with the following challenge: For a string $s$, define $f(s)$ as the number of its substrings that also appear in the dictionary. You are given $q$ queries. In each query, you are given an integer $n$. You must calculate the following sum: $$ \sum_{x \in St} f(x) $$ Where $St$ is the set of all lowercase strings of length $n$. Since the number can be very large, print the result modulo $10^9 + 7$. A substring is a contiguous segment of letters from a string. For example, "defor" is a substring of "codeforces", but "fors" is not. Help Baran and Thaer decode the secrets hidden within this enchanted lexicon.
sections_input: The first line of the input contains two integers, $m,q$ ($1\leq m,q \leq 100$) — the number of words in the dictionary, and the number of queries, respectively. Each of the following $m$ lines contains a string $s_i$ ($1\leq|s_i|\leq 100$) — the $i$-$th$ word of the dictionary. Each of the following $q$ lines contains a single integer $n_i$ $(1 \leq n_i \leq 10^{18})$ — the $i$-$th$ query. It is guaranteed that $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m |s_i|$ does not exceed $100$.
sections_output: For each query, print the answer modulo $10^9+7$ on a single line.

title: Moamen and the Ancient Geometry Scroll
sections_statement: One quiet evening, Moamen discovered an ancient scroll buried beneath the library floor of the old university. The scroll described a mysterious geometric figure — a puzzle once used by mathematicians of the past to test their brightest students. The figure involves two right-angled triangles $ABC$ and $BDE$, where the lengths $AB = BD = x$ and $AC = BE = y$. - Point $G$ is the intersection of segments $AC$ and $DE$. - Point $F$ is the intersection of segments $BC$ and $DE$. - $FH$ is a height in triangle $CFG$ dropped from point $F$ to side $CG$. - A circle is drawn centered at point $F$ with radius equal to $FH$. - Point $I$ is the intersection of the circle and the segment $FG$. The red region marked in the diagram represents a strange shape called $IHG$, and the scroll poses one final question to Moamen: What is the area of the shape $IHG$? The red area represents the shape $IHG$.
sections_input: The first line has a single integer $1 \le T \le 10^5$, the number of test cases. Each of the $T$ next lines has two integers $1 \le x \le y \le 10^9$.
sections_output: For each test case, output a single floating-point number representing the area of the shape $IHG$. Your answers must have a relative or absolute error of at most $10^{-4}.$

title: Maher and the Rabbit Exodus
topics_list: constructive algorithms, data structures, greedy, trees
sections_statement: A vicious wolf pack has cornered the Rabbit Tribe in their forest village. The village is represented as a rooted tree with $N$ houses and $N-1$ one-way roads. Every road leads away from the root. Each house contains some rabbits. A rabbit may move from its current house to any house in the subtree rooted at its current position, including the current house itself. There are three types of houses: 1. Thatched houses: every non-leaf house is of this type. 2. Stone houses: some leaf houses are made of stone. 3. Iron houses: the remaining leaf houses are made of iron. The wolves attack as follows: 1. They destroy every thatched house and catch every rabbit left inside it. 2. Then, they inspect all stone houses and destroy one stone house containing the maximum number of rabbits. If several stone houses have the same maximum number, any one of them may be destroyed. 3. Iron houses are safe. However, each iron house can contain at most $C$ rabbits. Determine the minimum possible number of rabbits caught by the wolves after moving the rabbits optimally.
sections_input: The first line contains two integers $N$ and $C$ $(2 \le N \le 10^5,\ 0 \le C \le 10^3)$, the number of houses and the capacity of each iron house. The second line contains $N$ integers $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_N$, where $p_1 = 0$, and $1 \le p_i < i$ for every $2 \le i \le N$. The value $p_i$ is the parent of house $i$. The third line contains $N$ integers $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_N$ $(0 \le A_i \le 10^4)$, where $A_i$ is the initial number of rabbits in house $i$. The fourth line contains $N$ integers $T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_N$ $(T_i \in \{1,2,3\})$, where $T_i$ is the type of house $i$. Every non-leaf house has type $1$, while every leaf house has type $2$ or $3$. If house $i$ has type $3$, then $0 \le A_i \le C$.
sections_output: Print one integer: the minimum possible number of rabbits caught by the wolves.

title: Career180 Configurator - Tailored Learning Track Builder
sections_statement: Career 180 is a leading Egyptian startup --- and a Den VC portfolio company --- that empowers youth across the Arab world to discover, prepare for, and pursue careers aligned with their strengths, goals, and market demand. Through personalized mentorship, bootcamps, and expert-led sessions, Career 180 helps students and early job seekers bridge the gap between education and employability. As part of a new initiative, Career 180 is launching a smart career track configurator. This tool generates a customized training plan for each user based on their available time, their individual specialization weight profile, and a large library of training subjects mapped to $36$ different specializations. The goal is to deliver the most impactful plan within the user's constraints. Each candidate has a percentage weight for each of the $36$ specializations, representing their relative focus. They also have a total number of hours $T$ they can dedicate to training. Career 180's subject library contains $n$ subjects. Each subject belongs to a single specialization $(1 \le s \le 36)$, has a duration in hours $(1 \le d \le T)$, and a raw benefit score $b$. The adjusted benefit for each subject is calculated as: $$ \text{AdjustedBenefit} = b \times \frac{\text{Weight of its specialization}}{100}. $$ You must select a set of subjects without repetition so that the total duration does not exceed $T$ and the total adjusted benefit is maximized.
sections_input: The first line contains two integers $n$ and $T$ $(1 \le n \le 10^4,\ 1 \le T \le 10^4)$ --- the number of available subjects and the total training time available to the candidate. The second line contains $36$ integers $w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_{36}$ $(0 \le w_i \le 100)$ --- the candidate's specialization weights in percent. Each of the next $n$ lines contains three integers $s$, $d$, and $b$ $(1 \le s \le 36,\ 1 \le d \le T,\ 1 \le b \le 10^4)$ --- the specialization index, duration, and raw benefit score for each subject.
sections_output: Print a single real number: the maximum total adjusted benefit, with at least $6$ decimal places.
sections_notes: In this sample, the user's weights give specialization $1$ a $20\%$ weight and specialization $2$ a $15\%$ weight. The optimal plan is to choose subject $1$ ($5$ hours, adjusted benefit $20.0$) and subject $2$ ($4$ hours, adjusted benefit $12.0$). This uses $9$ hours $(9 \le 10)$ and gives a total adjusted benefit of $32.0$.

title: The AI Time Bridge
topics_list: counting, sliding window, strings, two pointers
sections_statement: In the year 2040, $\textbf{Moamen}$ and $\textbf{Amr}$ find themselves in a world far beyond imagination. Artificial Intelligence has evolved to control entire cities, explore galaxies, and even simulate minds. After years of research, they manage to activate a mysterious invention: the $\textit{AI Time Bridge}$, a temporal portal that allows precise travel across time using high-level AI logic. As they explore the future, they receive an urgent alert --- the regional ECPC programming competition is about to start back in the year 2025. In that competition lies their chance to see a lot of wrong answers and they can't miss it. To return, the AI Time Bridge must be activated with a valid binary signal. The AI only permits $\textbf{good}$ binary substrings to fuel the jump back. A binary string $t$ is considered $\textbf{good}$ if, for any two $\texttt{1}$ characters, the number of $\texttt{0}$ characters between them is at least $k$. Given a binary string $s$ of length $n$, help Moamen and Amr count the number of good substrings that can power the time bridge and send them back to 2025 in time for ECPC.
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer $T$ ($1 \le T \le 10^3$), the number of test cases. Then $T$ test cases follow. The first line of each test case contains two integers $n$ and $k$ ($0 \le k < n \le 10^6$) --- the size of the binary string and the number of $0$ characters required between two $1$ characters. The second line of each test case contains a single string, the binary string $s$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $10^6$.
sections_output: For each test case, print a single integer --- the number of good substrings of $s$.

title: Permutation Secrets
sections_statement: Interactive Problem Houssain and Moamen love puzzles. One day, they stumbled upon a curious machine that hides a secret permutation $p$ of integers from $1$ to $n$. Moamen challenged Houssain to find the original position of the number $n$ in the hidden permutation. However, there's a twist — the only way to interact with the machine is through a limited set of queries. Can Houssain figure out where $n$ was originally located before any changes were made? Your task is to help Houssain identify the position of $n$ in the original permutation using at most $50 \times n$ queries. There are two types of queries: - Increment Query ? x This increases the value of $p_x$ by $1$ (i.e., $p_x := p_x + 1$). The interactor replies with the number of equal pairs in the current array. An equal pair is any pair $(i, j)$ with $i \lt j$ and $p_i = p_j$. - Answer Query ! i This query asserts that you believe the original permutation had $p_i = n$. The interactor replies with: 1 if your guess is correct, 0 if your guess is incorrect. After an answer query you can't make any more queries for that test case and you have to move to the next test case. You can make at most $50 \times n$ increment queries. The interaction for each test case begins by reading the integer $n$. To make an Increment Query, output a line in the following format: "? x" — $(1 \le x \le n)$, then the following happens: - Increases the value of $p_x$ by $1$ (i.e., $p_x = p_x + 1$). - The interactor replies with the number of equal pairs in the updated array. - An equal pair is any pair $(i, j)$ with $i \lt j$ and $p_i = p_j$. To make an Answer Query, output a line in the following format: "! i" — $(1 \le i \le n)$, This indicates that you believe $p_i = n$ in the original permutation. Then the interactor replies with: - 1 if your guess is correct. - 0 if your guess is incorrect, in this case your program should immediately terminate to receive the verdict Wrong Answer. Otherwise, it may receive any other verdict. Note that the answer query doesn't count in your limit of queries. If your program makes more than $50$ $\times$ $n$ queries, your program should immediately terminate to receive the verdict Wrong Answer. Otherwise, it may receive any other verdict. After printing a query, do not forget to output the end of the line and flush the output. Otherwise, you will get Idleness limit exceeded. To do this, use: - fflush(stdout) or cout.flush() in C++; - System.out.flush() in Java; - sys.stdout.flush() in Python;
sections_input: The first line contains a single positive integer $t$ $(1 \le t \le 1000)$, the number of test cases. Each test case contains a single positive integer $n$ $(1 \le n \le 1000)$, the size of the permutation. It is guaranteed that the sum of $n$ overall test cases doesn't exceed $2000$.
sections_output: Interactive problem — output queries and answer inside interaction protocol.

title: AI Simulation on Uncle Island
sections_statement: In the year 2125, Omar and George are lead researchers at the Virtual Earth Lab. Their latest project simulates an island environment called Uncle Island — a polygonal landmass on a 2D grid designed to study AI-driven population behavior. The island's shape is encoded as a simple polygon, where every interior angle is either $90^\circ$ or $270^\circ$. Inside this digital world, AI citizens occupy every integer point inside the polygon — each point represents a smart house with one autonomous resident. Each simulated morning, a random non-empty subset of AI citizens is selected by the training model to perform the daily task of resource foraging, analogous to fishing. Each selected citizen moves to the nearest coastal point — defined as a point with integer coordinates that lies on the polygon's edge. Movement is determined by Manhattan distance: $$ d = |p_x - q_x| + |p_y - q_y| $$ where $(p_x, p_y)$ is the AI citizen's location, and $(q_x, q_y)$ is the closest point on the island's edge. To optimize neural efficiency and energy modeling, Omar and George want to calculate: The expected value of the maximum distance walked by any AI citizen during a resource-foraging simulation, assuming each non-empty subset of citizens is equally likely to be chosen. Simulation snapshot of Uncle Island, from the Virtual Earth Lab. Can you help them compute this expected maximum distance?
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer $N$, the number of vertices of the polygon. ($4 \le N \le 2 \times 10^6$). Each of the next $N$ lines contains $p_x$ and $p_y$, the coordinates of the polygon points sorted in either clockwise or counterclockwise direction ($0 \le p_x, p_y \le 2 \times 10^3$). It is guaranteed that the polygon is simple, and each point shares its $x$ or $y$ with the previous point.
sections_output: Output a single value, the expected value of the largest distance walked by a single citizen modulo $998244353$. Formally, it can be shown that the answer can be expressed as an irreducible fraction $\frac{p}{q}$ where $p$ and $q$ are integers and $(q \neq 0 \mod 998244353)$. Output the integer $p.q^{-1} \mod 998244353$.

title: Jaber and the Prediction Tree
sections_statement: In the year 2040, Jaber is working with a smart AI-powered tree called the Prediction Tree. This tree has $n$ connected nodes, and each node can store some machine learning models. Each model is a simple formula of the form $Ax + B$. At the beginning, no node has any models. Let $S(v)$ be the set of models stored at node $v$. Jaber can reconfigure the tree by choosing any node $v$ to be the root. When he does that, the number of nodes in the subtree of another node $u$ (with respect to this new root $v$) is called $sub(u, v)$. Jaber wants to measure how good a model from $S(v)$ is when applied to the subtree size of $u$. He defines a score function $f(u, v)$ as: $$ f(u, v) = \min_{Ax + B \in S(v)} \left(A \cdot sub(u, v) + B\right) $$ He will give you $q$ queries to help him work with the tree: - 1 v A B — Jaber adds the model $Ax + B$ to node $v$. - 2 u — Jaber wants to know the smallest value of $f(u, v)$ over all nodes $v$ that have at least one model. Can you help Jaber answer all his queries?
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer $T$ ($1 \le T \le 10^5$) — the number of test cases. Each test case begins with a line containing two integers $N$ and $Q$ ($1 \le N, Q \le 10^5$) — the number of nodes and the number of queries. The next $N - 1$ lines each contain two integers $u$ and $v$ ($1 \le u, v \le N$), denoting an undirected edge between nodes $u$ and $v$. The next $Q$ lines contain the queries in one of the following formats: - 1 v A B — Add the line $Ax + B$ to $S(v)$. - 2 u — Output the minimum value of $f(u, v)$ over all $v$ with non-empty $S(v)$. It is guaranteed that the first query in each test case is of type 1. The total sum of $N$ and $Q$ over all test cases does not exceed $10^5$. All values of $A$ and $B$ satisfy $|A|, |B| \le 10^9$.
sections_output: For each testcase, for each query of the $2$nd type, output the answer in a separate line.

title: Temporal Signal Breakdown
sections_statement: In the year 2025, two curious engineers — Yasser and Ayman — are working on a top-secret AI-driven communication system that transmits data through multi-phase signals. Each signal is represented by an array of $n$ integers. To ensure signal stability, the AI system requires that the incoming signal can be split into three contiguous segments that pass through distinct decoder layers: - The first segment must have a MEX of 0. - The second segment must have a MEX of 1. - The third segment must have a MEX of 2. Formally, determine whether there exist two integers $x$ and $y$ ($1 \lt = x \lt y \lt n$) such that: $$ \text{MEX}(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_x) = 0 $$ $$ \text{MEX}(a_{x+1}, a_{x+2}, \dots, a_y) = 1 $$ $$ \text{MEX}(a_{y+1}, a_{y+2}, \dots, a_n) = 2 $$ Yasser believes that finding such a split would allow them to stabilize the temporal signal and open a gateway for ultra-low-latency AI learning across time zones. Ayman is skeptical — but intrigued. Help them determine whether such a split is possible. The MEX (minimum excluded) of an array is the smallest non-negative integer that does not belong to the array. For instance: - The MEX of $[2, 2, 1]$ is $0$, because $0$ does not belong to the array. - The MEX of $[3, 1, 0, 1]$ is $2$, because $0$ and $1$ belong to the array, but $2$ does not. - The MEX of $[0, 3, 1, 2]$ is $4$, because $0$, $1$, $2$, and $3$ belong to the array, but $4$ does not.
sections_input: Each test consists of multiple test cases. The first line contains a single integer $t$ $(1 \le t \le 10^4)$ — the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains three integers $n$ $(3 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)$ — the length of the array $a$. The second line of each test case contains $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ $(0 \le a_i \le n)$ — the elements of the array $a$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $2 \cdot 10^5$.
sections_output: For each test case, print "YES" (without quotes) if it is possible to split the array into three such parts as described. Otherwise, print "NO".

title: The Reflective Gauntlet
sections_statement: In the year 2149, technology has advanced beyond imagination. Two elite cyber-engineers, Moufeed and Baran, have developed the Reflective Gauntlet — a precision-targeting AI weapon that uses quantum bullets and advanced reflection systems to eliminate rogue AI drones threatening the orbital colonies. You are stationed at the control hub, positioned at the origin point $(0, 0)$. Using the Reflective Gauntlet, you must destroy $n$ fast-moving drones. Each drone appears at coordinates $(x_i, y_i)$ and remains visible for only $d_i$ time units before disappearing into stealth mode. The weapon fires at a constant unit speed and supports high-tech features: - Two vertical reflective walls are installed at $x = -L$ and $x = L$. When a bullet reaches either wall, it reflects perfectly — preserving its speed and angle, just like light in a mirror. - Additionally, a magnetic redirection system enables an intelligent one-time horizontal redirection when a bullet passes strictly above a target at height $y_i$. In such cases, the bullet may be redirected directly to the target along a straight path parallel to the x-axis at the same height $y = y_i$, if needed. The bullet follows a piecewise linear path made up of straight-line segments and wall reflections. Its travel time equals its total path length (since its speed is $1$). A drone is destroyed successfully if the bullet can reach it in time (within $d_i$). You must target all drones in the given order, one after another. Scoring: Each bullet's score is the number of straight-line segments in its path: - Includes the initial segment from the origin. - Adds one segment for each wall reflection. The magnetic redirection does not increase the score — it is considered part of the same segment and may only be used once per drone. Your mission is to calculate the maximum total score (sum of all shots) achievable while ensuring every drone is hit within its allowed time window.
sections_input: The first line contains two integers $n$ and $L$ — the number of drones and the half-distance between the reflective walls. $1 \le n \le 10^4$, $1 \le L \le 10^9$ Each of the next $n$ lines contains three integers: $x_i$, $y_i$, and $d_i$ — the drone's position and visibility time. $-L \le x_i \le L$, $1 \le y_i \le 10^9$, distance from (0, 0) to $(x_i, y_i)$ does not exceed $d_i$, and $d_i \le 10^{12}$
sections_output: Print a single real number — the maximum total score (sum of segments across all drone hits).
sections_notes: - The bullet reflects only off the vertical walls at $x = -L$ and $x = L$. - Only one magnetic redirection is allowed per shot, and only if the bullet passes above the target. - The redirection does not increase the score. - It is allowed to hit a target without using either wall reflections or magnetic redirection if a direct shot is sufficient.

title: Training Camp
sections_statement: Amr and Zezo are attending a competitive programming training camp in Cairo. After the official contest ends, their coach, Fegla, prepares one final challenge. There are $N$ problem sets. The $i$-th set initially contains $C_i$ unsolved problems and is worth $V_i$ points. Amr moves first. On each turn, the current player must choose a problem set containing at least one unsolved problem and solve exactly one problem from it. If the player solves the last remaining problem in that set, they win the set, score $V_i$ points, and immediately play another turn. A player may receive multiple consecutive extra turns in this way. Otherwise, their turn ends and the other player plays next. The game ends when all problem sets have been completed. Both players play optimally to maximize their own total score. Find the maximum total score Amr can obtain.
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer $T$ ($1 \le T \le 10^4$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $N$ ($1 \le N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$) — the number of problem sets. The second line contains $N$ integers $C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_N$ ($1 \le C_i \le 10^9$) — the initial number of unsolved problems in each set. The third line contains $N$ integers $V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_N$ ($1 \le V_i \le 10^9$) — the number of points awarded for winning each set. It is guaranteed that the sum of $N$ over all test cases does not exceed $2 \cdot 10^5$.
sections_output: For each test case, print a single integer — the maximum total score Amr can obtain if both players play optimally.

title: Supermask Sum
sections_statement: You are given two integers $n$ and $r$. Find an array $a = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_r)$ of $r$ distinct non-negative integers such that every $a_i$ is a supermask of $n$. An integer $x$ is called a supermask of $n$ if $(x \mathbin{\&} n) = n$, where $\mathbin{\&}$ denotes the bitwise AND operation. Determine the minimum possible value of $\sum_{i=1}^{r} a_i$. Since the answer may be large, print it modulo $10^9 + 7$.
sections_input: The first line contains one integer $T$ ($1 \le T \le 10^5$) — the number of test cases. Each of the next $T$ lines contains two integers $n$ and $r$ ($0 \le n \le 10^9$, $1 \le r \le 10^9$).
sections_output: For each test case, print one integer — the minimum possible sum of the array modulo $10^9 + 7$.

title: Endure Investments
sections_statement: Endure believes in backing exceptional founders who solve real problems and build companies that can endure. As an early-stage investment fund with roots in the entrepreneurial ecosystem, Endure evaluates many opportunities while managing the available investment capacity. In this problem, we model a simplified version of such a process. There are $N$ investment opportunities numbered from $1$ to $ N$. The $ i$-th opportunity becomes available at time $ A_i$, remains available until time $ E_i$ ($ E_i \gt A_i$), and yields a return of $ P_i$ units if it remains active until completion. Endure can actively support at most $ K$ investments at the same time, where $1 \le K \le N$. The opportunities arrive in strictly increasing order of their arrival times $ A_i$. They are processed according to the following rules: - Completion Phase: Before considering a new opportunity arriving at time $ A_i$, every active investment $ j$ with $ E_j \lt A_i$is considered successfully completed. It is removed from the active portfolio, and its return $ P_j$ is added to the total accumulated return. - Investment Phase: The new opportunity $ i$ is added to the active portfolio. - Capacity Phase: If the number of active investments becomes greater than $ K$, exactly one active investment must be dropped. The investment with the smallest return $ P$ is dropped. If several active investments have the same minimum return, the one among them with the earliest completion time $ E$ is dropped. A dropped investment contributes $0$ to the total return. After all $ N$ opportunities have arrived, all investments still remaining in the portfolio eventually complete successfully and contribute their returns. You are given a target return $ T$. Determine the minimum portfolio capacity $ K$ for which the accumulated return is at least $ T$. If the target cannot be reached even when $ K=N$, output $-1$.
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer $Q$ ($1 \le Q \le 10^4$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers $N$ and $T$ ($1 \le N \le 10^5$, $1 \le T \le 10^{14}$) — the number of workloads and the target total profit, respectively. The next $N$ lines each contain three integers $A_i, E_i, P_i$ ($1 \le A_i \lt E_i \le 10^9$, $1 \le P_i \le 10^9$) — the arrival time, expiration time, and profit of the $i$-th workload. Workloads are given in strictly increasing order of arrival times ($A_1 \lt A_2 \lt \cdots \lt A_N$). It is guaranteed that the sum of $N$ over all test cases does not exceed $2 \cdot 10^5$.
sections_output: For each testcase, output a single integer representing the minimum buffer capacity $K$ required to achieve a total profit of at least $T$. If it is impossible even with $K = N$, output $-1$.

title: Cosmic Harvest
sections_statement: You start at the point $(0, 0)$ on a two-dimensional plane. There are $n$ points. The $i$-th point is located at integer coordinates $(x_i, y_i)$. Multiple points may have the same coordinates. At each second, your position $(x, y)$ changes using exactly one of the following moves: - $(x, y) \to (x - 1, y + 1)$; - $(x, y) \to (x, y + 1)$; - $(x, y) \to (x + 1, y + 1)$. A move that changes the $x$-coordinate is called a diagonal move. Whenever your path visits coordinates containing one or more points, you collect all points at those coordinates. Each point can be collected at most once. Determine the following two values: - The maximum possible number of collected points. - Among all paths that collect the maximum possible number of points, the minimum possible number of diagonal moves.
sections_input: The first line contains one integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 1000$) — the number of points. Each of the next $n$ lines contains two integers $(-10^9 \le x_i \le 10^9$, $-10^9 \le y_i \le 10^9)$ — the coordinates of the $i$-th point.
sections_output: Print two integers $c$ and $m$, where: - $c$ is the maximum possible number of collected points; - $m$ is the minimum possible number of diagonal moves among all paths that collect exactly $c$ points.
sections_notes: In the first example, all three points lie on the line $x = 0$. By keeping the same $x$-coordinate at every second, the path visits $(0, 1)$, $(0, 2)$, and $(0, 3)$. Therefore, all $3$ points are collected using $0$ diagonal moves. In the second example, the points are located at $(1, 1)$, $(2, 2)$, $(3, 3)$, and $(4, 4)$. By increasing the $x$-coordinate by $1$ at every second, the path visits all four points. Therefore, the maximum possible number of collected points is $4$, and the minimum possible number of diagonal moves is $4$.

title: The Waleed Khalil Shuffle
sections_statement: The Waleed Khalil Prize challenge is back. After using numbers inspired by the birthdays of Dr. Amira Swilam and Dr. Mohamed Abo El Azm, Fouad prepared another challenge using the same two special patterns: 198 for Dr. Amira and 64 for Dr. Mohamed. This time, however, the digits are already written in a row, and Fouad is allowed to rearrange them only through adjacent swaps. He wants to determine which birthday pattern can be created with less effort. For each test case, Fouad has a string $S$ consisting entirely of digits (0-9). In one operation, Fouad can choose any two adjacent digits in the string and swap them. - Dr. Amira wins if Fouad can make the string contain 198 as a contiguous substring. Let $K_A$ be the minimum number of swaps required to achieve this. If this is impossible, define $K_A=+\infty$. - Dr. Mohamed wins if Fouad can make the string contain 64 as a contiguous substring. Let $K_M$ be the minimum number of swaps required to achieve this. If this is impossible, define $K_M=+\infty$. Fouad wants to use the absolute minimum number of swaps possible. Therefore: - If Dr. Amira's pattern can be formed and either Dr. Mohamed's pattern cannot be formed or $K_A \le K_M$, Dr. Amira receives the Waleed Khalil Prize. - Otherwise, if Dr. Mohamed's pattern can be formed and $K_M \lt K_A$, Dr. Mohamed receives the Waleed Khalil Prize. - If neither pattern can be formed because the required digits are not available, nobody receives the prize. Determine the winner for each test case.
sections_input: The first line contains an integer $T$ ($1 \le T \le 1000$) — the number of test cases. For each test case: - The first line contains an integer $N$ ($1 \le N \le 5000$) — the length of the string $S$. - The second line contains a string $S$ of length $N$, consisting only of digits (0-9). It is guaranteed that the sum of $N$ over all test cases does not exceed $5000$.
sections_output: For each test case, print a single line: - AMIRA $K$ if Dr. Amira receives the prize, where $K$ is the minimum number of swaps. - ABO $K$ if Dr. Mohamed receives the prize, where $K$ is the minimum number of swaps. - -1 if neither can receive the prize.

title: Coffee Cooldown
sections_statement: During a programming contest, Mnesy oversees a large reservoir that supplies coffee to the contestants. There are $n$ coffee machines connected to the reservoir. Machine $i$ operates during the time interval $[l_i, r_i)$. At time $t$, while machine $i$ is operating, its signed coffee flow rate is $$ R_i(t) = a_i(t-l_i)^2 + b_i(t-l_i) + c_i. $$ A positive rate means that the machine adds coffee to the reservoir, while a negative rate means that it removes coffee from it. Let $$ F(t) = \sum_{i:\,l_i \le t \lt r_i} R_i(t) $$ be the total flow rate at time $t$. The amount of coffee in the reservoir is increasing whenever $F(t) \gt 0$. Mnesy calls a time interval $[L, R]$, where $L \lt R$, a cooldown interval if, for every time $t$ with $L \lt t \lt R$ at which no machine starts or stops, both of the following conditions hold: - the amount of coffee in the reservoir is increasing; - the rate at which the amount of coffee is increasing is strictly decreasing. The exact instants at which one or more machines start or stop are ignored when checking these two conditions. Therefore, a cooldown interval may continue through such an instant if the conditions hold on both adjacent open time intervals. Help Mnesy find the maximum possible length $R-L$ of a cooldown interval.
sections_input: The first line contains one integer $n$ ($1\le n\le 2\cdot 10^5$) — the number of coffee machines. Each of the next $n$ lines contains five integers $$ l_i,\ r_i,\ a_i,\ b_i,\ c_i $$ ($0\le l_i \lt r_i\le 10^9$, $1\le r_i-l_i\le 1000$, $-5\le a_i,b_i,c_i\le 5$), describing machine $i$. Several machines may start or stop at the same time.
sections_output: Print one real number — the maximum possible length of a cooldown interval. Your answer will be considered correct if its absolute or relative error does not exceed $10^{-6}$. If no cooldown interval of positive length exists, print $0$.
sections_notes: - First testcase: The flow rate is $R(t) = -t^2 + 4t - 3$. It is positive for $1 \lt t \lt 3$ and strictly decreasing after $t = 2$. Therefore, the longest cooldown interval is $[2, 3]$, with length $1$. - Second testcase: The flow rate is $R(t) = t^2 + 5$. Although it is always positive, it is increasing for $t \gt 0$, so the rate at which coffee is added is not strictly decreasing. Hence, there is no positive-length cooldown interval. - Third testcase: For $0 \le t \lt 2$, the total flow rate is $F(t) = 3 - t$, which is positive and strictly decreasing. For $2 \le t \lt 4$, the second machine starts and $F(t) = 5 - t$, which is also positive and strictly decreasing. The instant $t = 2$ is ignored when checking the conditions, so the cooldown interval can continue across it. Thus, the entire interval $[0, 4]$ is a cooldown interval, giving the answer $4$.

title: Anas Forest
sections_statement: You are given a tree with $n$ vertices. The vertices are numbered from $1$ to $n$, and vertex $i$ has a positive integer value $a_i$. You may remove any number of edges from the tree. After removing these edges, the tree is divided into several connected components. A connected component is called good if the greatest common divisor of the values assigned to all vertices in the component is greater than $1$. The sum of a component is the sum of the values assigned to its vertices. Your task is to partition the tree into good connected components while satisfying the following conditions: - The number of connected components must be minimized. - Among all partitions with the minimum possible number of components, the maximum component sum must be minimized. If it is impossible to partition the tree into good connected components, print $-1$.
sections_input: The first line contains one integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 10^5$) — the number of vertices in the tree. The second line contains $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ ($1 \le a_i \le 10^5$) — the values assigned to the vertices. Each of the next $n - 1$ lines contains two integers $u$ and $v$ ($1 \le u, v \le n$, $u \ne v$) — the endpoints of an edge of the tree. It is guaranteed that the given edges form a tree.
sections_output: If it is impossible to partition the tree into good connected components, print $-1$. Otherwise, print two integers $c$ and $s$, where: - $c$ is the minimum possible number of good connected components; - $s$ is the minimum possible value of the maximum component sum among all valid partitions into exactly $c$ components.
sections_notes: In the first example, one optimal partition consists of the following components: - vertices $\{1, 2\}$, with values $\{6, 10\}$, greatest common divisor $2$, and sum $16$; - vertex $\{3\}$, with value $\{15\}$, greatest common divisor $15$, and sum $15$; - vertices $\{4, 5\}$, with values $\{7, 14\}$, greatest common divisor $7$, and sum $21$. The minimum possible number of good components is $3$. Among all valid partitions into $3$ good components, the minimum possible value of the maximum component sum is $21$.

title: Suitera Mosque
sections_statement: Suitera works with complex engineering geometries while building advanced electromagnetic and multiphysics simulation tools. Before one of Suitera's technical events, a prayer area is represented by a strictly convex quadrilateral. The quadrilateral is described by four vertices $P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4$, given in counterclockwise order. The direction of the qibla is along the positive $y$-axis, so all prayer rows must be placed on horizontal lines. All people must be placed within the quadrilateral, including its boundary. For the prayer arrangement, the following rules apply: - The vertical distance between any two consecutive prayer rows must be at least $d$. Formally, if the rows are placed at heights $c_1 \lt c_2 \lt \dots \lt c_k$, then $c_{i+1}-c_i \ge d$ for every $1 \le i \lt k$. - On every row except the uppermost row, the horizontal distance between any two adjacent worshippers must be at least $1$. - On every row except the uppermost row, the leftmost worshipper must be at least $1$ unit away from the left boundary of the quadrilateral at that height. - On every row except the uppermost row, the rightmost worshipper must be at least $1$ unit away from the right boundary of the quadrilateral at that height. - Horizontal and vertical positions may be real numbers. There is one special requirement. Yasser Arafat is the Imam, and he must be alone on the uppermost prayer row. Therefore, the uppermost row contains exactly one person: Yasser. Yasser may stand at any point belonging to the intersection of his row with the quadrilateral. The $1$-unit horizontal spacing and boundary-distance requirements do not apply to the Imam's row. Determine the maximum possible total number of people that can be placed, including Yasser.
sections_input: The first line contains an integer $t$ ($1 \le t \le 10$) — the number of test cases. Each test case is described as follows. The first line contains an integer $d$ ($1 \le d \le 10^4$) — the minimum vertical distance between two consecutive prayer rows. Each of the next four lines contains two integers $x_i$ and $y_i$ ($-10^4 \le x_i,y_i \le 10^4$) — the coordinates of vertex $P_i$. The vertices $P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4$ are given in counterclockwise order. It is guaranteed that the four vertices are distinct and form a strictly convex quadrilateral.
sections_output: For each test case, print a single integer — the maximum possible total number of people that can be placed while satisfying all the given conditions, including Yasser.
sections_notes: In the sample test case, the prayer area is a square with side length $10$, and $d=2$. Five ordinary prayer rows can be placed at heights $0$, $2$, $4$, $6$, and $8$. Each of these rows has horizontal width $10$. Therefore, each ordinary row can contain $$ \lfloor 10-1 \rfloor = 9 $$ worshippers while keeping at least $1$ unit from each side boundary and at least $1$ unit between adjacent worshippers. Yasser occupies the uppermost row alone at height $10$. Thus, the total number of people is $$ 5 \cdot 9 + 1 = 46. $$

title: Factorial Chains
sections_statement: You are given an integer $n$. Count the number of nonempty arrays $A = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k)$ that satisfy all of the following conditions: - $a_i \gt 1$ for every $1 \le i \le k$; - $a_i$ is divisible by $a_{i-1}$ for every $2 \le i \le k$; - $\prod_{i=1}^{k} a_i = n!$. Two arrays are considered different if they have different lengths or if they differ in at least one position. Print the number of valid arrays modulo $998244353$.
sections_input: The first line contains one integer $t$ ($1 \le t \le 2 \cdot 10^5$) — the number of test cases. Each of the next $t$ lines contains one integer $n$ ($2 \le n \le 5000$).
sections_output: For each test case, print one integer — the number of valid arrays modulo $998244353$.

title: Fouad's Family
sections_statement: Fouad has three very special birthdays in his family that he never wants to forget: - Celine's birthday is on 30/5; - Aceel's birthday is on 26/3; - Ahmed's birthday is on 23/8. Since Fouad loves both his family and numbers, he decided to create a classification system inspired by their birthdays. For a positive integer $n$, he checks whether it is divisible by the day of each birthday: - It is BEST if it is divisible by $30$, $26$, and $23$, meaning that it matches the birthday days of Celine, Aceel, and Ahmed. - Otherwise, it is GREAT if it is divisible by $30$ and $26$, matching the birthday days of Celine and Aceel. - Otherwise, it is GOOD if it is divisible by $30$, matching Celine's birthday day. - Otherwise, it is NORMAL. The categories are hierarchical, so Fouad always chooses the strongest category that applies. You are given $T$ positive integers. Determine Fouad's classification for each integer.
sections_input: The first line contains one integer $T$ ($1 \le T \le 100\,000$) — the number of test cases. Each of the next $T$ lines contains one integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 10^{18}$) — the integer to classify.
sections_output: For each test case, print exactly one of the following strings: - BEST if $n$ is divisible by $30$, $26$, and $23$; - GREAT if $n$ is divisible by $30$ and $26$, but not by all three numbers; - GOOD if $n$ is divisible by $30$, but does not belong to a stronger category; - NORMAL otherwise.

title: Boxes and Coins
sections_statement: You have two boxes, $A$ and $B$, both initially empty. The following process is performed for exactly $n$ days. On each day, one coin is added to one of the two boxes. The coin is added to box $A$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ and to box $B$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, independently of all previous days. At most once during the entire process, immediately after that day's coin is added, you may perform the following operation: - Choose one of the two boxes. - If the chosen box currently contains $x$ coins, replace the number of coins in it with $\left\lfloor \frac{x}{2} \right\rfloor$. You may also choose not to perform the operation at all. Let $a_i$ and $b_i$ denote the numbers of coins in boxes $A$ and $B$, respectively, after day $i$. These values are considered after both the coin addition and the optional operation on that day. Your score is the number of days $i$ such that $a_i \gt b_i$. Your decision whether to perform the operation, and which box to choose if you perform it, may depend on all coin placements observed up to that moment. Assuming that you play optimally, determine the maximum possible expected value of your score.
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer $t$ ($1 \le t \le 1000$) — the number of test cases. Each of the next $t$ lines contains a single integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 5000$) — the number of days. It is guaranteed that the sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $5000$.
sections_output: For each test case, output a single number — the maximum possible expected score. Your answer will be considered correct if its absolute or relative error does not exceed $10^{-6}$. Formally, let your answer be $a$, and the jury's answer be $b$. Your answer is accepted if and only if $\frac{|a - b|}{\max(1, |b|)} \le 10^{-6}$.
sections_notes: In the first test case ($n = 1$), one coin is added. With probability $0.5$ it lands in $A$ and $a_1 \gt b_1$; with probability $0.5$ it lands in $B$ and $a_1 \lt b_1$. The operation never helps on the very first day, so the expected score is $0.5$. In the second test case ($n = 2$), there are $4$ equally likely sequences: $AA$, $AB$, $BA$, $BB$. - $AA$: If we do not perform the operation, box $A$ leads on both days. Score $= 2$. - $AB$: After day $1$ we have $a=1,b=0$. After day $2$ we have $a=1,b=1$ (tie). Use the operation on $B$: $b$ becomes $\lfloor 1/2 \rfloor = 0$, so $a=1,b=0$ (lead). Score $= 2$. - $BA$: After day $1$ we have $a=0,b=1$. After day $2$ we have $a=1,b=1$ (tie). Use the operation on $B$: $b$ becomes $0$, we lead. Score $= 1$. - $BB$: $A$ never leads. Score $= 0$. Expected score $= (2 + 2 + 1 + 0) / 4 = 1.25$.

title: Samir's TikTok Journey
sections_statement: Samir had always dreamed of becoming a TikTok star, so he started his journey by rearranging everything around him—literally! His first vlog was all about finding the perfect arrangement, and now he needs your help to make it as impressive as possible. You are given an array $a$ consisting of $n$ integers, where $n$ is divisible by $4$. You can rearrange the elements of the array in any order you want. Let the rearranged array be $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$. Your task is to find a rearrangement $b$ that maximizes the value of: $$ S_1(b) = b_1 - b_2 + b_3 - b_4 + \dots + b_{n-1} - b_n $$ Among all rearrangements that achieve the maximum possible value of $S_1(b)$, you must choose one that also maximizes: $$ S_2(b)=b_1+b_2-b_3-b_4+\cdots+b_{n-3}+b_{n-2}-b_{n-1}-b_n. $$ If there are multiple such rearrangements, output any of them.
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer $t$ ($1 \le t \le 10^4$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each testcase contains a single integer $n$ ($4 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, $n \bmod 4 = 0$). The second line contains $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ ($-10^9 \le a_i \le 10^9$). It is guaranteed that the sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $2 \cdot 10^5$.
sections_output: For each test case, output $n$ integers $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$ — the rearranged array. If there are multiple optimal rearrangements, you may output any of them.

title: XOR Sort
sections_statement: Raad has an array of $n$ integers. He wants to make the array strictly increasing. Before applying any operation, Raad must choose a non-negative integer $x$. Then, for every index $i$, he may independently choose an integer $k_i$ such that $0 \le k_i \le x$, and replace $a_i$ with $a_i \oplus k_i,$ where $\oplus$ denotes the bitwise XOR operation. Determine the minimum possible value of $x$ such that the resulting array can be made strictly increasing.
sections_input: The first line contains a single integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$) — the number of elements. The second line contains $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ ($0 \le a_i \le 10^9$).
sections_output: Print a single integer — the minimum $x$ needed, or $0$ if the array is already strictly increasing.
sections_notes: In the first example, an array containing one element is already strictly increasing, so the answer is $0$. In the second example, choose $x=4$. We can take $k_1=4$ and $k_2=4$, obtaining $5 \oplus 4 = 1$ and $0 \oplus 4 = 4.$ The resulting array is $[1,4]$, which is strictly increasing. No value of $x \lt 4$ can make the array strictly increasing, so the answer is $4$.

title: Fractured Currents
topics_list: bitwise operations, dfs and similar, graphs
sections_statement: You are given an undirected graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. The vertices are numbered from $1$ to $n$, and vertex $i$ has a non-negative integer value $a_i$. The score of the graph is calculated as follows. For every pair of distinct vertices $(u, v)$ such that $u \lt v$ and there exists a path between $u$ and $v$, add $a_u \oplus a_v$ to the score, where $\oplus$ denotes the bitwise XOR operation. You must remove exactly one edge from the graph. After removing this edge, the score is recalculated using the remaining edges. Find the minimum possible score after removing exactly one edge. Since the answer may be large, print it modulo $10^9 + 7$.
sections_input: The first line contains two integers $n$ and $m$ ($1 \le n, m \le 10^5$) — the number of vertices and the number of edges, respectively. The second line contains $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ ($0 \le a_i \le 10^9$) — the values assigned to the vertices. Each of the next $m$ lines contains two integers $u$ and $v$ ($1 \le u, v \le n$) — the endpoints of an undirected edge. The graph may contain self-loops and multiple edges between the same pair of vertices.
sections_output: Print one integer — the minimum possible score after removing exactly one edge, modulo $10^9 + 7$.
sections_notes: In the first example, there is only one vertex, so there are no pairs of distinct connected vertices. Therefore, the score is $0$ both before and after removing the self-loop. In the second example, the graph is the path $1 - 2 - 3.$ If we remove the edge between vertices $1$ and $2$, only vertices $2$ and $3$ remain connected. The resulting score is $a_2 \oplus a_3 = 95 \oplus 71 = 24.$ If we remove the edge between vertices $2$ and $3$, only vertices $1$ and $2$ remain connected. The resulting score is $a_1 \oplus a_2 = 55 \oplus 95 = 104.$ Therefore, the minimum possible score is $24$.

title: AASTMT Cycles
sections_statement: This problem is dedicated with appreciation to AASTMT and its Regional Informatics Center for their long-standing commitment to competitive programming, their continuous support of generations of Egyptian contestants, and their remarkable contribution to the growth of the ICPC community in Egypt and the Arab region. For many years, the Arab Academy for Science, Technology and Maritime Transport (AASTMT), through its Regional Informatics Center, has played a major role in building and supporting the competitive-programming community in Egypt and the Arab region. Generation after generation of contestants has passed through contests organized and hosted with the support of AASTMT, from the Egyptian Collegiate Programming Contest to the regional and international stages. To celebrate this long journey, consider the generations of contestants as cycles. You are given an integer $n$ and an array $W_1,W_2,\ldots,W_n$. Consider any permutation $p$ of length $n$. Every permutation can be uniquely decomposed into disjoint cycles. For example, the permutation $$ p=[2,3,1,5,4] $$ consists of two cycles: $(1,2,3)$ and $(4,5)$, whose lengths are $3$ and $2$, respectively. The score of a cycle depends only on its length. A cycle of length $L$ has score $W_L$. The total score of a permutation is the product of the scores of all cycles in its decomposition. In other words, if the cycle lengths of a permutation are $L_1,L_2,\ldots,L_k$, then its score is $$ W_{L_1}\cdot W_{L_2}\cdots W_{L_k}. $$ Determine the sum of the scores of all permutations of length $n$. Since the answer may be very large, output it modulo $998244353$.
sections_input: The first line contains one integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 2000$). The second line contains $n$ integers $W_1,W_2,\dots,W_n$ ($0 \le W_i \lt 998244353$), where $W_i$ is the score of a cycle of length $i$.
sections_output: Output a single integer — the sum of the scores of all possible permutations of length $n$, modulo $998244353$.
